claims.text: Degradation of additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 during elevated-temperature gas exposure is governed by selective oxidation reactions.
High oxygen availability promotes formation of cohesive, protective oxide scales.
The protective oxide scales formed under oxidizing conditions are predominantly enriched in Cr and Ti.
Protective oxides form at grain boundaries and external surfaces.
The Cr- and Ti-enriched scales help maintain the integrity of the fcc matrix.
Reducing conditions cause protective oxides to be absent or unstable.
The absence or instability of protective oxides under reducing conditions leads to internal and localized oxidation.
Localized oxidation under reducing conditions occurs preferentially along grain boundaries.
Internal and grain-boundary oxidation degrades the alloy's mechanical performance.
The as-built additively manufactured alloy has an fcc-dominated microstructure.
The as-built alloy has cellular or columnar microstructural features.
The as-built alloy contains residual stresses characteristic of additive manufacturing.
The starting alloy has no significant pre-existing oxide scale.
Cr and Ti accumulate at grain boundaries and surfaces.
Cr- and Ti-enriched grain boundaries and surfaces act as oxide-nucleation sites and govern scale continuity and protectiveness.
Discontinuous grain-boundary oxidation compromises mechanical integrity through embrittlement or microcrack initiation.
Oxidizing exposure will produce a uniform, thin scale while preserving strength and fatigue resistance relative to the starting state.
Reducing exposure will produce localized internal oxide regions at grain boundaries and measurable losses in mechanical performance.
The proposed mechanism is expected to operate between 800 and 1000 °C for this alloy composition.
Lower temperatures or composition changes that alter oxide-forming tendencies may produce different degradation behavior.
